title: The Periodic Table
description: How elements are organised — groups, periods, trends, alkali metals, halogens, noble gases, transition metals, and the genius of Mendeleev's predictions.

notes.heading: Organisation of the Periodic Table
notes.body: The periodic table arranges all known elements in order of increasing atomic number (protons). Elements are organised into periods (horizontal rows) and groups (vertical columns). The period number tells you how many electron shells an atom has. The group number (for Groups 1-2 and 13-18) tells you how many electrons are in the outer shell. The table is divided into metals (left and centre) and non-metals (right), separated by a zigzag line starting below boron. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer shell electrons, which gives them similar chemical properties. Example: all Group 1 elements (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs) have 1 outer electron and are highly reactive metals. All Group 17 elements (F, Cl, Br, I) have 7 outer electrons and are reactive non-metals. Group 18 (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe) have full outer shells — they are the noble gases and are extremely unreactive (inert).

illustration.alt: A simplified periodic table showing periods, groups, metals, non-metals, and the zigzag metalloid boundary.
illustration.caption: The periodic table arranges elements by atomic number into periods (rows) and groups (columns).

notes.heading: Group 1: The Alkali Metals
notes.body: Group 1 metals (lithium Li, sodium Na, potassium K, rubidium Rb, caesium Cs) are soft, silvery metals with low density. They all have 1 electron in their outer shell and are extremely reactive — they must be stored under oil to prevent reaction with oxygen and water vapour. Reactivity INCREASES down the group: lithium fizzes gently in water; sodium melts into a ball and fizzes vigorously; potassium reacts violently, igniting the hydrogen gas produced with a lilac flame. Reaction with water: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. The metal hydroxide formed is alkaline (hence 'alkali metals'). Trend down the group: atoms get larger, the outer electron is further from the nucleus, the attraction is weaker, so the electron is lost MORE easily → reactivity increases. Physical trends down the group: melting/boiling points decrease, density generally increases. They form ionic compounds with non-metals (e.g., NaCl, KBr) and react with oxygen to form oxides (e.g., Na₂O).

illustration.alt: Atomic models of lithium, sodium, and potassium showing increasing atomic size down Group 1, plus sodium reacting with water.
illustration.caption: Group 1 metals get larger down the group, so the outer electron is lost more easily and reactivity increases.

notes.heading: Group 17: The Halogens
notes.body: Group 17 elements (fluorine F, chlorine Cl, bromine Br, iodine I, astatine At) are non-metals with 7 outer electrons. They exist as diatomic molecules (F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂). Reactivity DECREASES down the group: fluorine is the most reactive (pale yellow gas), chlorine (green gas), bromine (red-brown liquid at room temperature), iodine (dark grey solid — sublimes to purple vapour). Halogens react with metals to form salts (halide ions): 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl. A more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one from its compound: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ (chlorine displaces bromine, seen by colour change to orange/brown). This is a displacement reaction. Trend down the group: atoms get larger, the outer shell is further from the nucleus, so it is harder to attract an additional electron → reactivity decreases. Halogens are toxic and corrosive — chlorine was used as a chemical weapon in WWI. Uses: chlorine for water purification and bleach, iodine as antiseptic, fluorine in toothpaste (as fluoride).

illustration.alt: Diatomic halogen molecules with their room-temperature states and a displacement reaction between chlorine and potassium bromide.
illustration.caption: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules; a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one from its salt solution.

notes.heading: Group 18: The Noble Gases
notes.body: Group 18 elements (helium He, neon Ne, argon Ar, krypton Kr, xenon Xe, radon Rn) have full outer electron shells (2 for helium, 8 for the others). This makes them extremely stable and unreactive — they were once called 'inert gases'. They are all colourless, odourless gases at room temperature. Boiling points increase down the group (increasing atomic mass → stronger intermolecular forces). Uses: Helium — lighter than air, used in balloons and airships (non-flammable, unlike hydrogen). Neon — red-orange glow in advertising signs when electricity passes through. Argon — fills light bulbs (prevents tungsten filament from oxidising at high temperatures). Krypton and xenon — used in high-intensity lamps and flash photography. Radon — radioactive, can accumulate in buildings from granite bedrock (health risk). In 1962, xenon was forced to react with fluorine (XeF₄), proving that noble gases are not completely inert — but their reactivity requires extreme conditions.

illustration.alt: Electron shell diagrams of helium, neon, and argon showing full outer shells, plus uses of noble gases.
illustration.caption: Noble gases have full outer electron shells, making them extremely stable and unreactive.

notes.heading: Mendeleev and the Development of the Periodic Table
notes.body: Dmitri Mendeleev (1869) created the first widely accepted periodic table. Unlike earlier attempts that ordered elements by atomic mass, Mendeleev's genius was: (1) He arranged elements by atomic mass but swapped some elements (e.g., tellurium and iodine) to fit chemical properties — arguing that atomic masses must have been measured incorrectly (he was right). (2) He left GAPS for undiscovered elements and PREDICTED their properties based on trends in the group. For example, he predicted 'eka-aluminium' (below aluminium) — when gallium was discovered in 1875, its properties matched Mendeleev's predictions almost exactly (density predicted: 6.0 g/cm³; actual: 5.9 g/cm³). This predictive power convinced the scientific community. (3) He grouped elements with similar chemical properties in the same columns. The modern periodic table is arranged by atomic number (not mass), thanks to Henry Moseley (1913), who used X-ray spectra to determine atomic numbers. Mendeleev's table is a perfect example of how scientific models make testable predictions and gain acceptance when verified.

illustration.alt: Mendeleev's periodic table with gaps for undiscovered elements and a comparison of predicted eka-aluminium with discovered gallium.
illustration.caption: Mendeleev left gaps and predicted properties of undiscovered elements, such as gallium below aluminium.

notes.heading: Metals, Non-Metals and Metalloids
notes.body: About 80% of elements are metals. Metal properties: shiny (lustrous), good conductors of heat and electricity, malleable (can be hammered into sheets), ductile (can be drawn into wires), high melting and boiling points (except mercury — a liquid at room temperature), form positive ions (cations) by losing electrons. Non-metal properties: dull, poor conductors (often insulators — graphite/carbon is an exception), brittle when solid, lower melting/boiling points (many are gases at room temperature), form negative ions (anions). Metalloids (semi-metals) along the zigzag line (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals. Silicon is a semiconductor — it conducts electricity only under certain conditions (when 'doped' with other elements), making it essential for transistors and computer chips. Oxides: metal oxides are typically basic (e.g., Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH); non-metal oxides are typically acidic (e.g., SO₂ + H₂O → H₂SO₃ — acid rain).

illustration.alt: Periodic table regions for metals, non-metals, and metalloids, plus a comparison of their typical properties.
illustration.caption: Metals occupy the left and centre, non-metals the right, and metalloids lie along the zigzag boundary.

notes.heading: Transition Metals vs Group Metals
notes.body: The transition metals (the large central block, Groups 3-12) differ from Group 1 and 2 metals: (1) Harder, stronger, denser — e.g., iron, copper, gold vs. soft sodium (cut with a knife). (2) Much higher melting points — tungsten (W) melts at 3422°C, the highest of any metal; sodium melts at 98°C. (3) Less reactive — they do not react vigorously with water (iron rusts slowly over time; gold does not react at all). (4) Form coloured compounds — CuSO₄ is blue, Fe₂O₃ is red-brown, KMnO₄ is purple. Group 1 and 2 compounds are typically white or colourless. (5) Variable valency — iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺; copper forms Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺. Group 1 metals only form +1 ions. (6) Many transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts — iron in the Haber process (making ammonia), platinum/palladium in catalytic converters, nickel in hydrogenation. Key examples: iron (construction, haemoglobin), copper (electrical wiring, plumbing), zinc (galvanising steel to prevent rust), titanium (aircraft, hip replacements).

illustration.alt: Comparison of transition metals and Group 1 metals, with coloured compounds and variable valency examples.
illustration.caption: Transition metals are harder, less reactive, form coloured compounds, and can have more than one ion charge.

flashcards.definition: A horizontal row in the periodic table. The period number equals the number of electron shells in each atom.
flashcards.example: Sodium is in Period 3 — its atoms have 3 electron shells (2,8,1).

flashcards.definition: A vertical column. Elements in the same group have the same number of outer shell electrons and similar chemical properties.
flashcards.example: All Group 1 elements (Li, Na, K) have 1 outer electron and are highly reactive metals.

flashcards.definition: Soft, reactive metals with 1 outer electron. Reactivity INCREASES down the group. React vigorously with water to form alkaline hydroxides and H₂ gas.
flashcards.example: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. Potassium reaction is violent enough to ignite the hydrogen.

flashcards.definition: Reactive non-metals with 7 outer electrons. Exist as diatomic molecules. Reactivity DECREASES down the group. Form salts with metals.
flashcards.example: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂ — chlorine (more reactive) displaces bromine, turning the solution orange/brown.

flashcards.definition: Extremely unreactive gases with full outer electron shells. Helium (2), others (8). Used for inert atmospheres, balloons, and lighting.
flashcards.example: Argon fills incandescent light bulbs to prevent the tungsten filament from burning in oxygen.

flashcards.definition: The first widely accepted periodic table (1869), arranged by atomic mass with gaps for undiscovered elements. He correctly predicted properties of gallium and germanium.
flashcards.example: Mendeleev predicted gallium's density as 6.0 g/cm³; actual value = 5.9 g/cm³ — remarkably accurate.

flashcards.definition: Hard, dense metals in the central block (Groups 3-12). High melting points, form coloured compounds, good catalysts, variable valency.
flashcards.example: Iron (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) — red-brown rust; copper (Cu²⁺) — blue solutions; chromium (Cr³⁺) — green.

flashcards.definition: A more reactive halogen replaces a less reactive halogen from its salt solution.
flashcards.example: Cl₂ added to KBr → KCl + Br₂. Solution goes from colourless to orange-brown as bromine forms.

flashcards.definition: Reactivity INCREASES down Group 1: atoms get larger → outer electron further from nucleus → lost MORE easily.
flashcards.example: Lithium fizzes gently; sodium fizzes vigorously; potassium ignites with a lilac flame.

flashcards.definition: Reactivity DECREASES down Group 17: atoms get larger → outer shell further from nucleus → harder to ATTRACT an extra electron.
flashcards.example: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen; iodine is much less reactive.

flashcards.definition: An element with properties intermediate between metals and non-metals. Found along the zigzag line. Silicon is a semiconductor.
flashcards.example: Silicon (Si) conducts electricity only when 'doped' — essential for transistors and computer chips.

flashcards.definition: A molecule composed of two identical atoms bonded together. Halogens, hydrogen, nitrogen, and oxygen naturally exist as diatomic molecules.
flashcards.example: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ — 'Have No Fear Of Ice Cold Beer' is a common mnemonic.

questions.stem: An element is in Group 2 and Period 3. What is its electron configuration?
questions.explanation: Period 3 = 3 shells. Group 2 = 2 outer electrons. Configuration: 2 + 8 + 2 = 12 electrons (magnesium).

questions.stem: Why do elements in the same group have similar chemical properties?
choices: They have the same number of protons
They have the same number of electron shells
They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell
They have the same mass number
questions.explanation: Outer shell electrons determine reactivity. Same group = same outer electron count = similar chemistry.

questions.stem: Sodium reacts more vigorously with water than lithium. Why?
choices: Sodium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and held less tightly, so it is lost more easily
questions.explanation: Down Group 1, atoms are larger. The outer electron is further from the attractive nucleus → weaker hold → easier to lose → more reactive.

questions.stem: Chlorine water is added to potassium bromide solution. It turns orange-brown. Why?
choices: Chlorine (more reactive) displaced bromine: Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
No reaction — the colour is from chlorine
questions.explanation: A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one. Chlorine is above bromine in Group 17, so it displaces Br⁻, forming orange-brown Br₂.

questions.stem: Why was Mendeleev's periodic table more successful than earlier attempts?
choices: He used atomic number instead of atomic mass
He left gaps for undiscovered elements and accurately predicted their properties
He discovered all the elements himself
questions.explanation: Mendeleev's gaps and predictions (verified when gallium and germanium were discovered) proved the table's validity. Predictive power = good science.

choices: They have full outer electron shells — no tendency to gain, lose, or share electrons
questions.explanation: Full outer shells = stable electron configuration. There is no energetic drive to react. They are already at maximum stability.

questions.stem: Copper forms Cu⁺ and Cu²⁺ but sodium only forms Na⁺. Why?
choices: Copper is a transition metal — variable valency; Group 1 only forms +1
questions.explanation: Transition metals can lose different numbers of electrons (variable valency). Group 1 always loses exactly 1 outer electron.

questions.stem: A shiny solid conducts electricity and forms green-coloured compounds. It is most likely:
questions.explanation: Coloured compounds are a hallmark of transition metals. This could be chromium(III) (green), nickel(II) (green), or copper(II) (blue-green).

questions.stem: Iodine is added to potassium chloride solution. Will a reaction occur?
choices: No — iodine is LESS reactive than chlorine, so cannot displace Cl⁻
Yes — all halogens displace each other
questions.explanation: Down Group 17, reactivity decreases. Iodine is below chlorine → less reactive → cannot displace chloride ions. No reaction.

questions.stem: Silicon is a metalloid. What does this mean practically?
choices: It is a semiconductor — conducts electricity only under certain conditions, ideal for electronics
It reacts with all other elements
questions.explanation: Metalloids like silicon have intermediate conductivity. Doping with other elements creates transistors — the foundation of all modern electronics.

questions.stem: Element X reacts violently with water, producing an alkaline solution and H₂. Stored under oil. It is:
questions.explanation: Violent water reaction → H₂ + alkali (KOH) is characteristic of Group 1 metals. Storage under oil prevents air/water contact.

questions.stem: Who revised the periodic table to use atomic number instead of atomic mass?
questions.explanation: Moseley determined atomic numbers via X-rays, allowing the table to be ordered by protons. This resolved remaining inconsistencies.

questions.stem: Why does reactivity DECREASE down Group 17?
choices: Atoms get larger → outer shell further from nucleus → harder to attract an extra electron
The outer electron is lost more easily
More protons make them less reactive
Halogens become metallic down the group
questions.explanation: Larger atoms have outer shells further from nuclear attraction. Halogens react by GAINING electrons — the larger the atom, the harder it is to pull in an extra electron.

questions.stem: Which is a typical property of MOST non-metals?
questions.explanation: Non-metals are mostly brittle solids or gases, poor conductors. Graphite is the unusual exception — it conducts electricity.

questions.stem: Mendeleev swapped Te and I positions despite Te having higher atomic mass. Why?
choices: He trusted chemical properties: iodine is halogen-like (Group 17) and belonged there
questions.explanation: Mendeleev prioritised chemical behaviour over mass. He argued atomic masses must be wrong — confirmed later by Moseley's atomic number work.
